outcome: Disproved before the window and still disproved: Martí-Pete, Rempe and Waterman (arXiv 2108.10256, first posted 23 Aug 2021; author-accepted version Oct 2024; J. Amer. Math. Soc. 38 (2025) 877-918) constructed transcendental entire functions with a bounded connected component of the escaping set, so the conjecture as worded is false. Since 26 Jan 2024 the events are the Oct 2024 accepted version, the 2025 JAMS publication, a July 2025 survey that restates the result, a March 2026 major revision of an unrelated Rempe-Gillen paper, and a Sept 2026 expository note by the same authors that re-presents the single-point case and discloses AI use in its drafting.
problem_asks: The bullet, as frozen on 26 Jan 2024: every connected component of the escaping set I(f) = {z : f^n(z) -> infinity} of an entire transcendental function f is unbounded. Unpacked: (1) a universal claim over all transcendental entire f, with no restriction on order, singular values or function class; (2) about the connected components of the escaping set I(f) itself, not of its closure (the closure version was established by Eremenko in 1989 per secondary sources); (3) the claim is that each such component is unbounded. Equivalently, the bullet asks whether some transcendental entire f has a bounded connected component of I(f). Nothing else is asked.

events.what_happened: Eremenko, 'On the iteration of entire functions', Banach Center Publications 23 (1989) 339-345, introduces the escaping set for transcendental entire functions and poses the question. Per secondary sources (Wikipedia Escaping set, the Bergweiler-Rempe survey excerpt, and a Martí-Pete talk summary cited in search results) he proved that every component of the closure of I(f) is unbounded and that the boundary of I(f) is the Julia set, and asked/conjectured that every component of I(f) itself is unbounded (the bullet's claim). The 1989 paper itself was not readable here; the Purdue status page links it as esc.pdf, which came back as an unreadable PDF.
events.delivers: Proves, per secondary sources, that every component of the closure of I(f) is unbounded, and that J(f) = boundary of I(f). Poses the components-of-I(f) question as a conjecture; proves nothing about it.
events.remains: The whole bullet: every component of I(f) being unbounded for all transcendental entire f.
events.time_since_posted: Not applicable: this is the posing event. Later engagement is recorded in the events below.
events.direction: Poses the question. The bullet's claim is the conjecture that the 1989 paper asks about; the paper does not assert a counterexample or a proof of it.

events.what_happened: Rippon and Stallard, 'On questions of Fatou and Eremenko', Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 133(4) (2005) 1119-1126, as cited in search results and in the scanned PDF page labels. The abstract text below comes from a search-result excerpt; the PDF is scanned images and was not readable: I(f) has at least one unbounded component; if f has a Baker wandering domain, I(f) is connected and unbounded.
events.delivers: Every transcendental entire f has at least one unbounded component of I(f). For f with a Baker wandering domain, I(f) is connected and unbounded, so the bullet holds for those f. Restriction: 'at least one' is weaker than 'every'; the Baker-domain result is a restricted class.
events.remains: Every component of I(f) for general f.

checked_by.who: Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. referee process
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication (volume and pages as cited in search results; not verified against the journal page)

events.time_since_posted: About 21 years by 2026; the journal listing is the only check recorded.
events.direction: Partial positive result for the bullet's claim (at least one unbounded component, all components in the Baker-domain case). Does not contradict the claim.

events.what_happened: Rempe, 'On a question of Eremenko concerning escaping components of entire functions', arXiv math/0610453 (v1 15 Oct 2006; v2 16 Mar 2007), Bull. London Math. Soc. 39 (2007) no. 4, 661-666, DOI 10.1112/blms/bdm053. The abstract (opened) says: for entire f with bounded singular set and bounded postsingular set, every component of I(f) is unbounded; it gives a partial answer to a question of Eremenko.
events.revisions: v1 15 Oct 2006; v2 16 Mar 2007 (final, minor changes); journal BLMS 2007.
events.delivers: For entire f with a bounded set of singular values and a bounded postsingular set, every component of I(f) is unbounded. Restriction: both boundedness hypotheses; the paper calls this a partial answer.
events.remains: Every component of I(f) for entire f that fails either boundedness hypothesis, which includes the class of the 2021 counterexample.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication (BLMS 39 (2007) 661-666, per the arXiv journal reference)

events.time_since_posted: About 20 years by 2026; no later comment found.
events.direction: Partial positive result for the bullet's claim under two boundedness hypotheses. Does not contradict the claim.

events.what_happened: Rottenfusser, Rückert, Rempe and Schleicher, 'Dynamic rays of bounded-type entire functions', arXiv 0704.3213 (v1 24 Apr 2007; v2 28 Feb 2009), Ann. of Math. 173 (2011) 77-125. Per the abstract (opened): constructs an entire function in the Eremenko-Lyubich class B whose Julia set has only bounded path-components, answering negatively a 1989 question of Eremenko; shows that for many finite-order functions in B every escaping point can be joined to infinity by a curve of escaping points. The question answered is the strong (curve) form, not the components form in the bullet.
events.delivers: Disproves the strong form (every point of I(f) joined to infinity by a curve in I(f)) for some class-B function; proves the strong form for many finite-order class-B functions. Does not address whether components of I(f) are unbounded.
events.remains: The bullet, untouched: whether every component of I(f) is unbounded.
events.direction: Answers a different question (the strong curve form) negatively. Neither confirms nor refutes the bullet's components claim.
events.object: An entire function f in the Eremenko-Lyubich class B whose Julia set has only bounded path-components (per the abstract, explicit construction not described in the abstract). Its escaping set does not give a counterexample to the components question.

events.what_happened: Rippon and Stallard, 'Baker's conjecture and Eremenko's conjecture for functions with negative real zeros', arXiv 1112.5103 (v1 21 Dec 2011; no journal reference on the arXiv page). Per the abstract (opened): both Baker's conjecture and Eremenko's conjecture (all components of the escaping set are unbounded) hold for many transcendental entire functions whose zeros all lie on the negative real axis, including those of order less than 1/2.
events.delivers: Eremenko's components claim holds for many entire functions with all zeros on the negative real axis, including those of order below 1/2. Restriction: the zero-location class; the abstract does not specify 'many' further.
events.remains: The bullet for functions outside this class, including the class of the 2021 counterexample.
events.time_since_posted: About 15 years by 2026; no journal reference found on the arXiv page, so journal status is not established.
events.direction: Partial positive result for the bullet's claim. Does not contradict it.

events.what_happened: Rippon and Stallard, 'Boundaries of univalent Baker domains', arXiv 1411.6999 (v1 25 Nov 2014; no journal reference on the page). Per the abstract (opened, abstract only): a new sufficient condition for the escaping set of f to be connected, and 'a new general result on Eremenko's conjecture'. The theorem statements were not read.
events.delivers: Unclear from the abstract alone. The abstract says it gives a new general result on Eremenko's conjecture for univalent Baker domains; I did not read the theorem, so I cannot say which components it controls.
events.remains: Not determinable from the abstract; probably the bullet for the class of functions with univalent Baker domains, but unverified.
events.time_since_posted: About 12 years by 2026; no journal status found.
events.doubts: The theorem statement was not read, so the scope of the 'general result on Eremenko's conjecture' is unknown here.
events.direction: Unknown from the abstract. Not established to contradict or support the bullet.

events.what_happened: Rippon and Stallard, 'Eremenko points and the structure of the escaping set', arXiv 1703.11001 (v1 31 Mar 2017). Per the abstract (opened): if I(f) is disconnected, then for any open disc D meeting the Julia set, I(f) minus D has uncountably many unbounded components; for the core A_R(f) of the fast escaping set, either it is connected with spider's-web structure or it has uncountably many unbounded components. The journal listing (Trans. AMS 2019) appeared in search results but was not opened.
events.delivers: Conditional on I(f) being disconnected, uncountably many unbounded components remain after removing a disc. Restriction: the disconnected case. Says nothing about bounded components when I(f) is connected.
events.remains: The bullet in the case where I(f) is connected, and the bounded-component question in general.
events.time_since_posted: About 9 years by 2026. Journal listing not opened.
events.direction: Partial structural results on the escaping set, conditional on disconnectedness. Does not contradict the bullet.

events.what_happened: Nicks, Rippon and Stallard, 'Eremenko's conjecture for functions with real zeros: the role of the minimum modulus', arXiv 1810.07814 (v1 17 Oct 2018; no journal reference on the page). Per the abstract (opened): for many families of transcendental entire functions, if the iterated minimum modulus m^n(r) tends to infinity for some r > 0, then I(f) is a spider's web, hence connected, so Eremenko's conjecture holds; the paper also gives new families where the condition holds and where it fails. The families are not named in the abstract.
events.delivers: For the families where the iterated minimum modulus condition holds, I(f) is connected and the bullet holds. Restriction: the iterated minimum modulus condition, for families the abstract does not name.
events.remains: The bullet for functions where the condition fails, including the 2021 counterexample family.
events.time_since_posted: About 8 years by 2026; no journal status found.
events.direction: Partial positive result for the bullet's claim. Does not contradict it.

events.what_happened: Martí-Pete, Rempe and Waterman, 'Eremenko's conjecture, wandering Lakes of Wada, and maverick points', arXiv 2108.10256. Versions: v1 23 Aug 2021; v2 4 Feb 2022; v3 29 Jun 2022; v4 5 Apr 2024; v5 30 Oct 2024 (author-accepted manuscript; the v5 comment says Section 9 was restructured and there was general revision). Journal: J. Amer. Math. Soc. 38 (2025) 877-918, DOI 10.1090/jams/1049 (per the Purdue status page, the Wikipedia citations and the arXiv comments; the AMS page returned 403). The paper's Conjecture 1.1 is the bullet's claim. Theorem 1.2 (v5 numbering): for any non-empty full connected compact set X there is a transcendental entire f with X a connected component of I(f). Theorem 1.3 (as cited by the 2026 note): there is a transcendental entire f with I(f) having a connected component consisting of a single point. The paper also gives the Lakes of Wada result (infinitely many Fatou components sharing one boundary) and maverick-point results (opened abstract page and v5 HTML).
events.revisions: v1 23 Aug 2021; v2 4 Feb 2022; v3 29 Jun 2022; v4 5 Apr 2024; v5 30 Oct 2024 (author-accepted manuscript, Section 9 restructured); JAMS 38 (2025) 877-918 (online date not verified).
events.delivers: Refutes the bullet's universal claim: there exist transcendental entire f whose I(f) has a bounded connected component, indeed a singleton {0} (Theorem 1.3 as cited in the 2026 note), and more generally every full connected compact set X is a component of I(f) for some f (Theorem 1.2). Restrictions the paper states or implies: the constructed functions have infinite order and lie outside class B (Remark 7.5, per my reading of the v5 text); the theorem does not give finite-order or class-B counterexamples. The construction is inductive (Arakelyan approximation, approximation lemmas, conformal-map estimates; Theorem 7.1 in v5), and I did not check the proof.
events.remains: Nothing of the bullet's universal claim: it is refuted. Still open per the paper: whether the conjecture holds for finite-order functions in class B, which the paper cites as known via RRRS11 and asks (Question 1.15) whether the restriction can be dropped. Those restricted questions are not what the bullet asks.

events.time_since_posted: About 5 years 1.5 months since v1 (23 Aug 2021) at 11 Oct 2026; about 2 years since the author-accepted v5 (30 Oct 2024). Independent expert write-ups (beyond the journal, the originator's status page, the authors' own talks and the authors' own 2026 note) were not found.
events.directly_checkable: Not by hand from the summary: the counterexample is not an explicit formula. It is an inductively constructed function (Arakelyan approximation); checking requires the v5 proof, which I did not verify.
events.doubts: (1) The arXiv v1 PDF was unreadable, so I could not confirm the counterexample is in v1; the date 23 Aug 2021 rests on the v1 submission date plus Wikipedia's statement that a 2021 paper constructed the counterexample. The v5 comment says Section 9 was restructured after v4, so the first version carrying the construction may be later than v1. (2) I read the v5 HTML up to about 200k of 206.5k characters; it was cut inside Section 9, so references and final sections were not read. (3) The paper is 43 pages and I did not verify the proof. (4) Scope wording risk: Rempe's Purdue talk abstract (a verse abstract) describes Eremenko's question as joining each escaping point to infinity by a connected set of escaping points, which is the strong curve form, not the components form the paper proves against (Conjecture 1.1). The components counterexample therefore answers the bullet, but the talk abstract's wording points at the other question. No erratum, corrigendum or withdrawal was found in searches.
events.direction: Cuts against the bullet's claim: exhibits transcendental entire functions with a bounded connected component of I(f), a singleton {0} and, more generally, any full connected compact set as a component.
events.object: A transcendental entire function f for which I(f) has a connected component consisting of a single point {0} (Theorem 1.3 as cited in the 2026 note), and, for any non-empty full connected compact set X, a transcendental entire f with X a component of I(f) (Theorem 1.2). Non-explicit: an existence theorem from an inductive approximation construction (Arakelyan's theorem plus approximation lemmas and conformal-map estimates); the functions have infinite order and are outside class B (Remark 7.5).

events.what_happened: Brown, 'Slow-growing counterexamples to the strong Eremenko conjecture', arXiv 2405.08811 (v1 14 May 2024; v2 8 Jan 2025; v3 15 Dec 2025; v4 12 Jul 2026 per the page). Per the abstract (opened, abstract page only): constructs class-B counterexamples to the strong form (every point of I(f) joined to infinity by a curve in I(f)) with slower growth, under a regularity assumption and a condition on a function Theta with Theta(t) to 0.
events.revisions: v1 14 May 2024; v2 8 Jan 2025; v3 15 Dec 2025; v4 12 Jul 2026 (current, per page).
events.delivers: Further counterexamples to the strong curve form, which was already disproved in 2011. Does not address the components question, and does not claim to resolve the original conjecture.
events.remains: The bullet, untouched by this paper.
events.time_since_posted: About 2 years 5 months by 2026; no review recorded.
events.direction: Different question (the strong form), with counterexamples that are consistent with the bullet's claim. Neither settles nor changes the bullet.
events.object: Transcendental entire functions in class B with slow growth (log log|f(z)| = O((log|z|)^(1+Theta(log|z|)))) for which some point of I(f) cannot be joined to infinity by a curve in I(f); constructed by adapting tracts of Benítez and Rempe. Explicit or non-constructive is not stated in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Bergweiler and Rempe, 'The escaping set in transcendental dynamics', arXiv 2507.11370 (v1 15 Jul 2025 only). Survey. The abstract (opened) says it explains the role of the escaping set, summarises main results and identifies open questions. The full text was not readable: the PDF exceeded the fetch size limit and the mirror was unreachable. Per search-result excerpts (not opened in full) the survey states the MRW counterexample as a theorem that {0} is a connected component of I(f) for some transcendental entire f, and describes Eremenko's conjecture as false in general.
events.delivers: Per excerpts only: restates the MRW singleton counterexample. Adds no new mathematics that I could see.
events.remains: Per the MRW event, nothing of the bullet's claim. Survey open questions were not read.
events.time_since_posted: About 15 months by 2026. Not an independent check: co-author Rempe is an author of the 2021 counterexample.
events.doubts: Full text not read, so the survey's exact wording and citation of the 2021 result are unverified.
events.direction: Restates the counterexample (per excerpts): cuts against the bullet's claim.

events.what_happened: Rempe, 'Arc-like continua, Julia sets of entire functions, and Eremenko's Conjecture', arXiv 1610.06278 (v1 20 Oct 2016; v2 24 Oct 2016; v3 12 Apr 2018; v4 21 Dec 2019; v5 4 Mar 2026, 'major revision from V4', with the second half significantly revised). Per the abstract (opened): studies Julia continua of disjoint-type entire functions (span zero; arc-like) and constructs one entire function whose Julia set has components on which iterates tend to infinity pointwise but not uniformly; the abstract says this 'is related to' Eremenko's conjecture on escaping sets. It does not say it proves or disproves that conjecture. The abstract's 'Eremenko's conjecture' phrase is not stated in full.
events.revisions: v1 20 Oct 2016; v2 24 Oct 2016; v3 12 Apr 2018; v4 21 Dec 2019; v5 4 Mar 2026 (major revision, second half significantly revised). Whether the pointwise-not-uniform construction is in v1 or was added in v5 was not checked.
events.delivers: On the Julia continua of disjoint-type functions; the Eremenko-related construction is a Julia-set result (iterates tend to infinity pointwise but not uniformly), not a statement about components of I(f). Restriction: disjoint-type functions.
events.time_since_posted: About 10 years since v1; the 4 Mar 2026 v5 major revision is the in-window change; no public review found.
events.doubts: I read only the abstract. The paper's relation to the bullet is stated only as 'related to'. The date of the relevant construction depends on whether it was in v1 or added in v5.
events.direction: Related but different question (Julia continua; pointwise-not-uniform escape on Julia components). Does not directly bear on the bullet's components claim.

events.what_happened: Martí-Pete, Rempe and Waterman, 'A counterexample to Eremenko's conjecture', arXiv 2609.21977 (v1 18 Sep 2026; 10 pages, 1 figure; math.DS, math.CV; no journal reference). An expository note, based on Rempe's lecture at the 2026 International Congress of Basic Science, that introduces the problem for a general audience. Per the abstract and the introduction (opened via the HTML page): it restates that the earlier paper (arXiv 2108.10256) constructs functions whose escaping set has prescribed compact components, including a singleton, which disproves the conjecture; it says its own proof of the single-point result differs from the JAMS paper's in two ways (a function built to have a wandering domain with the escaping point on its boundary, and a direct sketch of the single-point proof rather than the JAMS framework for wandering compact sets); and it sketches a variant with a prescribed half-strip as an oscillating wandering domain with an escaping point on its boundary. Theorem 1.3 of the note (per its quotation): there is a transcendental entire f such that I(f) has a connected component consisting of a single point.
events.delivers: Re-establishes the singleton case: some transcendental entire f has {0} (a single point) as a component of I(f), by a construction the note presents as more direct. Adds the half-strip variant as a sketch. Nothing beyond the 2021 event for the bullet's claim.
events.remains: Nothing of the bullet's claim, which the 2021 event refutes. The note does not address the finite-order or class-B restriction.
events.time_since_posted: About 3 weeks (18 Sep 2026 to 11 Oct 2026). No independent reading found yet; the note is by the authors of the 2021 result.
events.directly_checkable: The singleton example is a transcendental entire function with a point as an escaping-set component; the note's direct proof might be checkable by hand, but I did not read it (the PDF was unreadable and I read the HTML summaries only).
events.doubts: Written by the authors of the 2021 result, so not independent; not refereed as far as I can see; the full text was not read by me directly (the PDF was binary and the HTML extraction was produced by a summarising fetch). The proof sketch was not checked.
events.direction: Cuts against the bullet's claim, re-presenting the singleton counterexample (the same direction as the 2021 event).
events.object: A transcendental entire function f for which the escaping set I(f) has {0} as a connected component (single point), built so that a prescribed half-strip is a wandering domain with an escaping point on its boundary (in the variant it sketches). Non-explicit: an existence construction; the note sketches a direct proof.

disputes.summary: Wikipedia pages date the counterexample differently. The Escaping set article says that in 2021 a paper by Martí-Pete, Rempe and Waterman constructed a counterexample, and its reference list dates the arXiv preprint 2024-10-30 (the v5 date). The Alexandre Eremenko article says a counterexample was found in 2025 and cites the JAMS paper. Eremenko's own status page cites JAMS 38 (2025). These are different events of the same paper (arXiv v1 2021; accepted v5 2024; JAMS 2025), not a priority dispute: no competing claimant was found. The date recorded here is the v1 submission date, with the v1 content unverified (see the 2021 event's doubts).

The Escaping set article (as fetched) still lists 'Can the escaping set of a transcendental entire function have a bounded component?' as an unsolved problem, while the same article reports the 2021 counterexample and says the escaping set can contain no curves in some examples. The article is internally inconsistent on this point. Its cached state at fetch time is what was read; no dated revision was checked.

Rempe's talk abstract on the Purdue site (a verse abstract, undated on the page) describes Eremenko's question as whether each escaping point can be joined to infinity by a connected set all of whose points escape. That is the strong curve form, not the components form in the bullet. The counterexample answers the components form; the curve form was disproved earlier (RRRS 2011). Anyone reading the talk alone could take the wrong question.

summary: Found: the bullet's claim is false. Martí-Pete, Rempe and Waterman (arXiv 2108.10256; first posted 23 Aug 2021; v5 author-accepted 30 Oct 2024; J. Amer. Math. Soc. 38 (2025) 877-918) construct transcendental entire functions for which a non-empty full connected compact set is a component of the escaping set, in particular a singleton {0}. That refutes the bullet exactly as worded, and it is the only event that settles the bullet. Its status was checked in these places: the arXiv abstract page (all versions, comments and the JAMS reference), the v5 HTML (about 200k of 206.5k characters read, cut inside Section 9, so the references and final pages were not read), Eremenko's own problem page (which marks the item Solved and cites JAMS 2025), and the Wikipedia articles. The v1 PDF was unreadable, so whether v1 already contains the construction is unverified; the 2021 date depends on that. The JAMS landing page returned 403 (the DOI redirects to it), so the online publication date and the final printed text were not checked. The journal volume and pages (38 (2025) 877-918) come from the arXiv journal-reference field, Eremenko's page and the Wikipedia citations, which agree; the arXiv comment only says 'To appear in JAMS'. A journal referee reviewed the paper (the acknowledgement thanks 'the referee'), and the originator's problem page marks it solved; no independent published expert write-up was found, and no erratum or withdrawal turned up in searches. A later expository note by the same three authors (arXiv 2609.21977, 18 Sep 2026) re-presents the singleton case, with a direct sketch and a variant, and carries an end-matter AI disclosure. Everything else is either pre-window partial results (Rippon-Stallard 2005; Rempe 2007 under bounded singular and postsingular sets; Rippon-Stallard 2011 for negative real zeros; Rippon-Stallard 2014 and 2017, the latter conditional on disconnectedness; Nicks-Rippon-Stallard 2018 under an iterated minimum-modulus condition) or results on different questions: the strong curve form (RRRS 2007/2011, with Brown 2024 giving slow-growing class-B counterexamples to that form), the closure version (1989), and Julia-set results (Rempe-Gillen, whose v5 major revision of 4 Mar 2026 is in the window but concerns Julia continua, not the components). The 2025 Bergweiler-Rempe survey restates the counterexample; I only read its abstract, so that restatement is from search excerpts. AI: the 2021 paper and the sources I read name no AI system (none_found true, with the unread tail noted in incomplete). The 2026 note names 'Generative AI (Microsoft 365 Copilot)' for drafting and language refinement and 'Claude Opus 5' for minor copy-editing suggestions and for creating Figure 1 at the authors' instructions, and states that 'AI tools did not supply new mathematical arguments'. Under 5.4 these uses are not load-bearing, so ai.systems is empty for that event and none_found is false. The AI searches (queries 6, 11-18, 30) and checks (the AlphaEvolve paper 2511.02864, the 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' survey 2608.29595, and an AI-solved-problems list at theneuron.ai) found no AI involvement in the mathematics of this problem. Close calls: (a) the date of the counterexample (2021 v1 vs 2024 v5 vs 2025 JAMS); I record 2021 because the first public written argument is the v1 submission, but the v1 text is unverified; (b) whether the 2026 note's 'Figure 1' and copy-editing are 'work done around the mathematics' (I judge yes, per the authors' own statement). Talks, not events: a Liverpool seminar (March 2023, search excerpt), Waterman's slides dated 2 July 2024 (search excerpt; the ICMS host was unreachable), the Geneva seminar of 17 Feb 2026 (abstract opened), the Purdue verse abstract (opened), and a 2026 ICBS lecture (not located). Each is dated to the written argument, so none is recorded separately.
competing_reading: (1) The counterexample's functions have infinite order and lie outside class B (Remark 7.5, per my reading). If the bullet were read as restricted to finite-order functions or class B, it would be open. The paper itself records that the conjecture is known for finite-order class-B functions and asks whether the class restriction can be dropped (Question 1.15). The bullet carries no such restriction, so I do not read it that way. (2) The 2021 date could move later if the construction first appeared in v5 (the Oct 2024 accepted version, which restructured Section 9) or in the JAMS version. The event would then be dated late 2024, inside the window, and it would still settle the bullet; only the window placement would change. (3) The Purdue verse abstract describes the strong curve form; a reader who takes that abstract as the target question would consider the components result to answer a different question. The paper's own Conjecture 1.1 is the components form.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The arXiv v1 PDF text (2108.10256v1) to confirm that the counterexample and its theorem numbers were already in v1, which would fix the 2021 date. (b) The JAMS published article or landing page (DOI 10.1090/jams/1049) for the online-first date and the final statement of the theorems. (c) The last 6.5k characters of the v5 HTML (Section 9 end, references, acknowledgements) to confirm there is no AI, software or computer-assistance statement beyond the one referee sentence seen. (d) The full text of the 2026 note (2609.21977), readable as text, to confirm the AI disclosure wording verbatim and the direct proof it sketches. (e) The full text of the Bergweiler-Rempe survey (2507.11370) to see how it states the result and cites it. (f) The Waterman ICMS slides (July 2024) to confirm the date of the first public talk on the construction.
